I get a lot of people who say that they don't understand technology because they're old. I usually pass that off as they just don't want to learn. The other day, I hit a wall with an older user and MS Excel.

Our user called in rather early in the morning, just after the "I forgot my password over the weekend," Monday morning rush. This particular user (who has the help desk playing Paper, Rock, Scissors to decide who takes his calls) was having trouble with a formula in Excel. Understanding that he probably did not make the spreadsheet, I skipped over those questions and got straight to the issue he was having. "What's going on with the spreadsheet?" I asked.

"I can't get the spreadsheet to save."

"What's your client IP?" We post those on the desktop so it's easy for users to find them.

"10.1.whatever."

"OK, can you show me what happens when you try to save?" I like to let the users drive unless I have to. They tend to remember how we solved a problem better that way.

"What do you mean?"

"Well, I'd like you to show me what happens when you try to save the file. That's the issue you're having, correct?"

"I'm not following what you're saying."

"Show me the issue you're having, please." I'm certain that my voice has conveyed lost patience at this point.

"I'm sorry, I'm lost on what you're asking me to do."

Forcing myself to calm down, "OK, sir. You said you have a problem with saving your file. I want you to show me what happens when you try to save."

"Oh! You want to see what happens when I'm saving the file?"

I sigh deeply, "Yes, sir."

...

So, now the new catch-phrase at work when a user is having trouble with our instructions is, "Show me!"
Was the user aware that you were seeing his screen?
Yes, we ask for the user's IP address and tell them it's, "so we can see what [they] see."
